extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, managers, and PR students preparing speeches, media appearances, and printed communications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing, rehearsing, delivering, evaluating, and repurposing speeches (and associated press/materials) in public relations contexts, including media training and use of visual aids and brochures.

rubrics_metrics.name: All-important introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening of the speech is crucial for gaining audience attention and empathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include a humorous anecdote, an ominous opening statement, intriguing little-known facts, or a revealing bit of personal history. Choose an opener appropriate to tone and audience. Example: an ominous opening for a serious speech: 'Central Valley may be a ghost town ten years from now...'. Intriguing facts can raise curiosity (e.g., 'Every year twenty-seven pounds of soot and dust particles fall on each citizen...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of humor — threefold test
rubrics_metrics.description: Three rules of thumb for using jokes or humor in a speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A joke should (1) be deliverable effectively by the speaker, (2) flow out of the speaker's experience, and (3) be appropriate to the subject. If these tests are met, levity can gain attention and empathy. Test jokes in rehearsal and omit humor that 'falls flat' or feels canned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anecdotes and personal stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Use anecdotes drawn from the speaker's experience to open or enliven a speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw anecdotes out during initial interviews and shape them into lively opening remarks. If an anecdote fails in rehearsal or embarrasses the speaker, leave it out. Even if a personal story doesn't win big laughs, it may help put the speaker at ease and establish rapport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone-appropriate openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Match the opening device to the intended tone of the speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For serious topics, an ominous or somber opening may be appropriate; for lighter occasions, a humorous anecdote or charming personal reflection may work. Ensure the opening fits the speech's subject and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: How much to say — time management
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan speech length with audience tolerance in mind and allow time for Q&A when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences are less patient than in the past; a speaker scheduled for 25 minutes who speaks 20 is usually acceptable. Narrow the topic so you can be complete yet brief. If commissioned for an hour, consider planning to devote half to questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research the audience composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze who the listeners are and what they know, care about, and might ask.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR should advise the speaker on audience makeup, interest level, prior knowledge, and likely questions so the speech can be tailored to the listeners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide coaching and preparatory sessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Make rehearsal and coaching an official part of preparing spokespeople.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some executives will welcome coaching, others may be insulted—consider making 'prep session' policy. Use professional consultants (often with videotape) to conduct training and give constructive feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attire appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Advise speakers on appropriate dress for the occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss proper attire—senior execs may already have a signature look, but technical staff may need guidance (e.g., scientists should avoid loud sportcoats at professional meetings). Take into account conference customs (e.g., resort/golf attire).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage stage fright and relaxation techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that some apprehension is useful but severe stage fright needs help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A certain amount of nervousness energizes performance. If apprehension is severe and paralyzing, consider a speech consultant to teach relaxation and coping methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish delivery during rehearsal
rubrics_metrics.description: Coach pacing, breathing, and opening delivery to increase effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Help the speaker slow delivery of the first lines; mark script where breaths should be taken; use positive reinforcement and substitute self-fulfilling prophecies ('You're going to do great...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Dry runs and videotaping
rubrics_metrics.description: Use in-house performances and videotape to rehearse and analyze delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide opportunities to perform before internal groups; videotape dry runs for instant analysis and as training archives for future speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual aids — primary purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual aids should primarily make the presentation clearer and secondarily add interest and variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They should not be used to compensate for a mediocre speaker. Decide on visual aids after completing research and a first draft; analyze whether data lend themselves to graphic display (slides, film, videotape).

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual aids — appropriateness to venue
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure chosen visual aids are compatible with the meeting room and equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm room can be darkened for slides, provide easels and nonreflecting signboards readable under harsh lighting, and consider lighted professional easels where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misuse of visual aids — anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid common mistakes that alienate or confuse the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not leave one card on an easel for thirty minutes if it's unnecessary; avoid cramming so much information that the speaker must flip cards too quickly; ensure visibility and interpretability from the audience's seats. Consider using a flip pad and felt-tip pen to create fresh, audience-tailored material. Recognize that a dynamic speaker may be better without visual aids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use live feedback during presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage real-time audience feedback to improve understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key benefit of a live spokesperson is the ability to acknowledge listener signals and adjust explanations. Videotape dissemination is an option for overly mechanical speakers, but live speakers should be coached to read and use feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coach reading audience perplexity and managing interruptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach speakers to notice audience confusion and to manage persistent questioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During rehearsal, train speakers to identify puzzled expressions and to stop and explain briefly. Teach stock phrases to ask audiences to hold questions ('...so I'll ask you please to hold your questions for just a few moments').

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech-evaluation checklist (use and design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a tailored checklist to evaluate speeches methodically, with space for specific comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide extra space/margins for evaluators' remarks; tailor items to organizational needs. The form should be used immediately after the speech for useful feedback. Example items (from Exhibit 24-1): room set-up; clarity of introduction; speaker dress and bearing; voice level; rapport; credibility; eye contact; avoidance of overdependence on script; opening attention; clarity of topic and main point; repetition/emphasis of main points; effective summary/ending; audience engagement; feedback acknowledged; opportunity for questions; visual aids set up and effective; speaker comfortable using aids; positive audience reaction. Use the checklist rather than delayed verbal briefings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for multiple uses of the speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare the speech so it can be repurposed for press distribution and other media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider writing the press release before the speech to distill key news thoughts. Provide the release and text to wire services and local media ahead of time. Be prepared to put the speaker in phone contact with reporters immediately after the speech. Consider reprinting speeches in booklet form or sending reprints to attendees for lasting impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizing a speakers bureau
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up an ongoing service to present organizational ideas through trained speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential elements: identify managers who enjoy and do the job well; assemble a set of topics that relate to organizational goals and are suitable for community groups; develop publicity/promotional systems (flyers, newsletters, mailing lists); and assign a booking person to handle requests and fulfill obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brushfire speakers bureau for rapid-response topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a temporary, focused speaker service for urgent PR issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an issue (e.g., proposed legislation) arises, set up a task force to arrange quick bookings via phone contacts with schools and civic groups to present the organization's viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stock speeches by institutional organizations (military example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare standard speeches and materials for routine commemorative occasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military branches prepare stock speeches for Veterans Day, Memorial Day, Fourth of July, etc., providing commanders with ready materials to increase visibility and reputation in communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing managers for press contacts — mock interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice media interviews using role-play to expose managers to hostile or awkward questioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage mock interviews or press conferences with PR staff acting as reporters and simulate rudeness, interruptions, hostile questions, and 'no-win' questions so the real event seems more manageable. Review good and bad media clips as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media interview guidelines (brief, honest, cordial, manage negatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key rules for handling reporters and interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Be brief — reporters favor succinct quotes; rambling leads to paraphrase or omission. 2) Avoid being 'cagey' or asking for off-the-record guarantees; prefer 'I am not at liberty to release that information at this time' and offer to follow up. Don't tell half-truths. 3) Maintain a firm but cordial stance; use proper forms of address and avoid favoritism toward friendly reporters. 4) When asked negative questions, avoid knee-jerk defensive answers — answer honestly and fully, explain what happened and what is being done to rectify it, and try to turn the reply into a positive for your view (symmetric model: truthful, full answers). 5) Keep calm and manage a smile — you're doing your job and so are the reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective interpersonal communication — listening and two-way dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize listening and create genuine two-way communication both inside and outside the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As organizations adopt the two-way symmetric model, PR must facilitate dialogue. Consider using third-party consultants to open dialogues with suspicious publics. Recommended activities: small-group sensitivity training, an ombudsman program for complaints/suggestions, and focus sessions with representatives of publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use confirming letters to translate verbal understandings into action
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide written confirmation of interviews, meetings, or agreements to ensure follow-through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A confirming letter creates a written record, helps assure organizational objectives are being achieved, and increases the practitioner's influence by 'creating reality' within the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brochures, fact sheets, and direct mail — mailing-list targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use mailing lists to target precisely the audiences you want to reach with printed materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mailing lists allow selecting homeowners, hobbyists, registered voters, senior citizens, supporters/opponents of causes, etc. Lists can be bought, exchanged with noncompeting organizations, or developed internally (event participants, requesters, contributors, customers, officials). Commercial direct-mail houses can handle list procurement and mailing for a fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of direct-mail formats and names
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the many formats (circulars, folders, booklets, pamphlets, broadsheets, pseudo-magazines) and select terminology appropriate to the audience and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government and regulated industries often prefer the term 'fact sheet' for dignity. Examples include wallet cards, stickers, looseleaf fact sheets, and agency bulletins. Choose format and name to suit occasion and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common brochure formats and folding choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard brochure sizes and panel configurations influence design and mailing efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common are two-fold six-panel (six panels each 3 5/8 x 8 1/2 inches), four-panel single-fold, and 8 1/2 x 22-inch travel-style sheets. Consider a teaser flap, pocket flaps for inserts, poster-sized spreads, and printer-efficient layouts. Choose format based on information amount, desired reading sequence (linear vs. random), design personality, and budget.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management considerations — brochures and fact sheets as controlled media
rubrics_metrics.description: Controlled media let PR present messages without media gatekeepers, supporting objectives like retention and exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because PR controls content and distribution, brochures/fact sheets support retention and cognitive change among active publics. They are less effective for passive publics unless mailed; passive readers may treat direct mail as junk and not read it. Use these formats when you want to communicate details the media might filter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best use case — active vs passive publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Match printed communication channels to the audience's level of activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brochures and fact sheets are excellent for active, information-seeking publics who will request or pick them up; they are less effective for passive publics unless direct-mailed (which still demands effort from the recipient). Consider complementary channels (radio/TV) to reach passive audiences.
